title: Readiness and Timeline at a Glance
lede: The burner (Aegis) is a design-and-simulation study today; a test burner is targeted around 2032 and a commercial unit around 2036, gated on four honest physics items.
body: Aegis is not a built machine. It is a design-and-simulation study of a deuterium–helium-3 (D–3He) tandem-mirror generator: 26.49 T plug field, 17 T throat, a 5.44% neutron fraction, and direct energy conversion in place of a steam cycle. Every performance figure quoted across this site is a modelled result, not a demonstrated one.

The dependency that sets the clock

Aegis cannot be decoupled from the breeder (Hyperion). The breeder begins construction in Q2 2027 and targets first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium around 2030; that tritium decays into the helium-3 the burner runs on. Only after the breeder is producing does a burner fuel supply exist at all. A test burner follows around 2032 and a commercial unit around 2036.

We do not hide the open items. Four physics gates stand between the present design and a fielded machine: the plug coil is overstressed roughly 3–3.9x at the design bore; the plug plasma regime sits 166–830x beyond any operated device; a single commercial unit demands about 400x today's domestic helium-3 supply; and modelled availability of 0.86–0.995 is 30–100x short of hyperscale Tier III uptime (0.99982). These are physics facts, not marketing caveats.

Read this section as a status report, not a sales pitch. Aegis is a low-neutron D–³He generator, not aneutronic; its story is resilient sovereign power for a fixed defense installation, independent of the fuel-logistics tail. That story only holds if the four gates close in hardware, so the pages that follow spend more words on the open items than on the finished physics.
See the four burner gates and simulated vs demonstrated for how each is being addressed.

title: We Are at the Design-and-Simulation Stage
lede: No burner hardware exists yet; Aegis is a closed set of physics and engineering models, and we label every number as modelled rather than measured.
body: At this stage the machine lives entirely in models: equilibrium and transport codes for the plasma, finite-element stress models for the magnets, neutronics for the 5.44% neutron fraction, and system models for direct energy conversion. There is no vessel, no coil, no plasma. The value of this stage is that it exposes the binding constraints before any metal is cut.

A design study is worth publishing when it is honest about its own maturity. The plug coil stress result (3–3.9x over the design bore) and the regime extrapolation (166–830x beyond operated devices) are findings of the simulation, and they are the reason the roadmap is staged rather than promising near-term power.
What would move us off this stage
A plug-coil coupon or sub-scale magnet that demonstrates field and stress margins
A helium-3 supply path that produces kilograms per year, not grams
A regime-scaling experiment that reduces the 166–830x extrapolation
An integrated test burner around 2032 that operates the full fuel-to-DEC chain
Until those exist, no net-gain claim is made for burner hardware. The first hardware net-gain milestone on the whole program belongs to the breeder FOAK around 2030, not to Aegis.

Calling this a design study is not a hedge; it is the accurate description. The equilibrium, transport, neutronics, and structural models are internally consistent and reproduce the physics we can check, but consistency is not the same as demonstration. The 26.49 T plug, the 17 T throat, and the 5.44% neutron handling are all targets the models set, and only hardware can confirm them.

title: Simulated Versus Demonstrated
lede: A line-by-line separation of what the models predict from what has actually been shown in hardware, on this program or elsewhere.
body: Confusing a modelled result with a measured one is the most common way fusion claims mislead. Below, each burner capability is tagged: done where hardware exists somewhere in the field, simulated where only models support it, and open where neither yet applies.

Where the field has real hardware

The D–3He reaction itself is textbook physics, and direct energy conversion of charged particles has been demonstrated at small scale in earlier mirror experiments. Those are not in dispute. What is unproven is the combination at the Aegis design point: the plug field, the confinement regime, and the fuel supply all at once.

Everything specific to the Aegis design point — the 26.49 T plug, the 17 T throat, the integrated fuel-to-DEC chain — is simulation. The test burner around 2032 is the first step that converts the middle rows of the ledger from simulated toward demonstrated.

The value of this ledger is that it never lets a modelled number borrow the credibility of a measured one. Anyone can read down the column and see exactly which rows rest on operated hardware and which rest on codes. As the program advances, rows move upward one at a time, each promotion backed by a specific test rather than by a revised assumption.

title: Reading the Readiness Levels
lede: We map Aegis onto the standard nine-level technology readiness scale so the design stage is not overstated.
body: Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) run from 1 (basic principles observed) to 9 (system proven in operation). They are a common yardstick precisely because they resist optimism: a working model is not a working machine.

Underlying D–³He physics: high, well established
Direct energy conversion concept: mid, bench heritage exists
Plug magnet at 26.49 T design bore: low, stress-infeasible as drawn
Integrated tandem-mirror at the design regime: low, not yet operated
Full plant availability: low, no operating data

Aegis spans a wide TRL band because its physics inputs are mature while its integrated hardware is not. The program's job over 2027–2036 is to lift the low subsystems — magnets, confinement regime, fuel supply, availability — without overstating the whole. The test burner around 2032 is a step, not a finish line; commercial readiness around 2036 requires the whole system, not just the physics.

The wide band is the honest signal here. A machine whose physics inputs are mature but whose integrated hardware is immature will always show a spread, and hiding that spread behind a single optimistic level is how programs mislead. Every subsystem in the low part of the band — magnets, confinement regime, fuel supply, availability — has a named experiment attached to it in this section.

title: The Four Burner Gates
lede: Four physics gates separate the present burner design from a fielded machine; each is stated with its measured magnitude, never softened.
body: Why we lead with the gates

Trust in a design study comes from stating its limits precisely. Aegis has four, and every one is a physics finding from our own models. None is an economic statement; we never translate a gate into a cost.

At the design bore the plug coil is overstressed by roughly 3–3.9x. As specified it is infeasible; the field of 26.49 T cannot be held by the coil as drawn. See the plug-stress gate.
The plug operating regime is 166–830x beyond any device ever run, so it cannot be post-dicted from existing data. See the regime gate.
Gates three and four — fuel and uptime

None of these four numbers is an economic statement, and we never convert one into a cost. They are distances measured in the models between the current design and a machine that could be fielded. A reader can use them as a checklist: each has a dedicated page explaining what it is, why it is hard, and the specific evidence that would shrink it.

A commercial unit needs about 400x today's domestic helium-3 (why breeder-bred and lunar 3He matter), and modelled availability of 0.86–0.995 is 30–100x short of hyperscale Tier III (0.99982). See the fuel gate and the availability gate.

title: Gate One in Depth: Plug Coil Feasibility
lede: At the 26.49 T design bore the plug magnet is overstressed by roughly 3 to 3.9 times its allowable, making the coil infeasible exactly as currently drawn.
body: The tandem-mirror end plugs must produce 26.49 T to confine the central-cell plasma electrostatically. At the bore the design requires, the structural stress in the conductor and its support runs about 3–3.9x the allowable for the materials assumed. That is not a tuning problem; it is a statement that the coil as specified cannot survive its own field.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 110" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="6" y="24" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">what exists today</text><rect x="6" y="30" width="70" height="18" rx="3" fill="#9FB1C4" opacity="0.6"/><text x="6" y="74" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">what one unit needs</text><rect x="6" y="80" width="590" height="18" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="600" y="94" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">~3–3.9x over allowable</text></svg>
Why it is a hard gate

Magnet stress scales steeply with field and inversely with bore. You cannot simply thicken structure without pushing bore, current density, and quench behaviour into their own limits. The 26.49 T plug is the single most demanding structural requirement in the machine.
Higher-strength structural alloys and reinforced winding packs
REBCO high-temperature superconductor operated with more conservative current density
A revised bore/field trade that lowers peak stress while preserving confinement
Sub-scale coil coupons tested to the modelled stress to validate margins
None of these is proven at 26.49 T today. The plug-coil prototype program is the route from this simulation result to a testable coil. See closing the plug-stress gate.

The plug-stress result is the reason the whole roadmap is staged rather than aggressive. A coil that cannot survive its own field is not a detail to be optimised later; it is a question that must be answered before an integrated machine is committed. We treat a possible outcome — that the design point itself must move — as legitimate rather than unthinkable.

title: Gate Two in Depth: A Regime Beyond Any Device
lede: The plug plasma sits 166 to 830 times beyond the operating point of any mirror ever run, so its behaviour cannot be post-dicted from existing data.
body: Confidence in plasma performance normally comes from post-dicting operated machines and extrapolating modestly. The Aegis plug asks for an operating point 166–830x beyond the envelope of any tandem mirror that has ever run. At that distance, no code can be said to be validated for the regime; the prediction is an extrapolation, not a fit.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><text x="250" y="33" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Operated mirror envelope</text><rect x="258" y="21" width="21.1" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="285.1" y="33" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">reference</text><text x="250" y="67" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Aegis plug (low est.)</text><rect x="258" y="55" width="267.7" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="531.7" y="67" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">166x</text><text x="250" y="101" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Aegis plug (high est.)</text><rect x="258" y="89" width="352.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="616.0" y="101" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">830x</text></svg>

Transport, stability, and micro-instability physics can change character across such a span. A model tuned to today's devices may miss loss channels that only appear at the Aegis point. This is why we call the plug performance un-post-dictable today rather than uncertain-but-likely.
Stepwise experiments that walk the regime outward and shrink the extrapolation
Cross-code benchmarking with explicit uncertainty bounds
A test burner around 2032 that operates far closer to the design point than any prior mirror

An extrapolation of this size is qualitatively different from ordinary uncertainty. Within the range of operated devices, a validated code can be trusted a little beyond its data; at 166–830x, the physics itself may change character, introducing loss channels no current model represents. That is why we describe the plug performance as un-post-dictable today rather than merely uncertain.
See closing the regime gate and regime-scaling experiments.

title: Gate Three in Depth: Helium-3 Supply
lede: A single commercial burner would demand roughly 400 times today's entire domestic helium-3 supply, so the fuel does not yet exist at terrestrial scale.
body: Deuterium is effectively unlimited; helium-3 is not. Today's domestic helium-3 comes mainly from tritium decay in aging stockpiles and is measured in small quantities. One commercial Aegis unit at steady state would need about 400x that entire supply. There is no market you can simply buy this from.

Why this shapes the whole program

This gate is the reason the breeder comes first. Hyperion breeds tritium at a ~4 kg/yr class, and that tritium decays into helium-3 (~1.97 kg/yr class) on a fixed physical clock. The burner fuel is therefore bred, not mined. Beyond a breeder fleet, lunar helium-3 is the only known reservoir at the scale a burner fleet would eventually require.
A breeder fleet sized to feed each burner it supports
Lunar helium-3 recovery as fleets scale (a multi-decade dependency)
Tight inventory accounting so no helium-3 is wasted in handling

This gate is the clearest illustration of why Aegis and Hyperion are one program, not two. A burner detached from a breeder has no fuel and no path to one; the ~400x gap cannot be bought around. Bred helium-3 makes the fuel real at unit scale, and lunar recovery is the only known reservoir that could ever make it real at fleet scale.
See the supply ramp plan, lunar dependency, and helium-3 from the breeder.

title: Gate Four in Depth: Availability Versus Tier III
lede: Modelled burner availability of 0.86 to 0.995 is 30 to 100 times short of hyperscale Tier III uptime at 0.99982, so Aegis is not a sole Tier-III source today.
body: Hyperscale data centers built to Tier III expect availability around 0.99982 — minutes of downtime per year. Modelled Aegis availability lands at 0.86–0.995. Expressed as downtime, that is 30–100x more outage than a Tier III facility tolerates. As a design study, Aegis cannot claim to be a lone Tier-III power source.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><text x="250" y="33" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Tier III target</text><rect x="258" y="21" width="352.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="616.0" y="33" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">0.99982</text><text x="250" y="67" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Aegis high est.</text><rect x="258" y="55" width="211.1" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="475.1" y="67" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">0.995</text><text x="250" y="101" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Aegis low est.</text><rect x="258" y="89" width="206.6" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="470.6" y="101" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">0.86</text></svg>
Why fusion availability is hard early

First-of-a-kind machines have unproven component lifetimes, maintenance intervals, and failure modes. The 5.44% neutron fraction, though low, still drives component wear that must be characterised before availability can be trusted. Availability is earned with operating hours, which do not exist yet.
What could close it, and the honest framing
Fleet operating hours that reveal and remove failure modes
Aegis paired with grid or storage rather than sold as a sole Tier-III feed

The comparison to Tier III is deliberately unflattering because pretending otherwise would be dishonest. A first-of-a-kind machine has no operating hours, and availability is a property you measure over years, not one you specify on a drawing. The credible near-term role for Aegis is as resilient sovereign power paired with grid or storage, not as a lone Tier-III feed.
See the availability roadmap and the gate summary.

title: Closing the Plug-Stress Gate
lede: The route from a 3-to-3.9x overstressed coil in simulation to a testable plug magnet: materials, current density, bore trades, and coupon testing.
body: Closing a structural gate is an engineering campaign, not a single fix. The plug-stress result (3–3.9x over allowable at the design bore) is attacked on several fronts at once, then validated in hardware coupons before any full coil is committed.

Higher-strength structural alloys with better fatigue behaviour
REBCO high-temperature superconductor run at conservative current density for margin
A bore/field trade that reduces peak stress while preserving central-cell confinement
Improved support structure and pre-stress management

No lever counts until a coupon or sub-scale coil is tested to the modelled stress and field. That test is what converts the plug from a simulation result to a demonstrated component, and it precedes the test burner around 2032.

Each lever in this campaign trades one constraint for another — more structure raises mass and cooling load, lower current density raises conductor volume — so the program optimises them together rather than in isolation. The discipline is that no combination is believed until a coupon or coil section is tested to the modelled stress at field. Analysis proposes; the coupon disposes.

title: Closing the Regime Gate
lede: Shrinking the 166-to-830x extrapolation by walking the operating point outward through staged experiments and disciplined cross-code benchmarking.
body: You do not close an extrapolation gate by asserting the model is right; you close it by shortening the distance the model must reach. Each experiment that operates closer to the Aegis point reduces the 166–830x multiplier and re-anchors the codes.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="6.0" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="81.2" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Today's mirrors</text><text x="81.2" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">1x baseline</text><line x1="156.5" y1="69" x2="174.5" y2="69" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="178.5" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="253.8" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Stepped campaigns</text><text x="253.8" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">walk outward</text><line x1="329.0" y1="69" x2="347.0" y2="69" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="351.0" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="426.2" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Test burner ~2032</text><text x="426.2" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">near design point</text><line x1="501.5" y1="69" x2="519.5" y2="69" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="523.5" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="598.8" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Commercial ~2036</text><text x="598.8" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">at design point</text></svg>
Measured transport and stability at progressively higher plug parameters
Explicit uncertainty bounds, not point predictions
Identification of any loss channels that appear only at high parameters
Re-validated codes at each step before the next extrapolation

Until such data exists, the plug regime remains un-post-dictable. The test burner around 2032 is the first machine intended to operate near the design point; commercial confidence around 2036 depends on what that machine measures.

The reason to walk the regime outward rather than leap to it is diagnostic, not cautious. A single jump to the design point would produce data no code predicted and teach little about why; incremental steps let each discrepancy be understood and fed back before the next step. The final extrapolation should be short enough that a technical reviewer would accept it.

title: Closing the Helium-3 Supply Gate
lede: Building a fuel supply from nothing at terrestrial scale: a breeder fleet first, then lunar helium-3 as burner fleets grow.
body: The ~400x supply gap is closed in two phases. First, a breeder fleet: each Hyperion breeds tritium that decays to helium-3, so burner fuel is produced domestically rather than bought. Second, as burner fleets scale beyond what breeders can feed, lunar helium-3 becomes the reservoir of last resort — a multi-decade dependency, not a near-term one.

The breeder produces the first kilograms; without it there is no burner fuel at all. Lunar recovery is only sensible once demand exceeds what a breeder fleet can supply, and its own logistics are unproven. Sizing the breeder fleet to the burners it feeds is the near-term engineering task.
Because every gram is bred, none can be wasted. Tight fuel accountancy and low-loss handling are part of closing this gate, not an afterthought.

Sequencing the two reservoirs correctly is itself part of closing the gate. Breeders must be built and reach FOAK before any burner fuel exists, so the near-term engineering task is sizing the breeder fleet to the burners it feeds. Lunar recovery is only rational once demand outgrows that fleet, and its own logistics remain unproven, so it anchors the long horizon rather than the near one.
See lunar dependency timeline and helium-3 from the breeder.

title: Closing the Availability Gate
lede: Turning modelled 0.86-to-0.995 availability into trusted uptime requires operating hours, redundancy, and honest positioning against Tier III.
body: The 30–100x uptime gap against Tier III (0.99982) cannot be closed on paper. It is closed by accumulating operating hours that reveal failure modes, then engineering them out. A first-of-a-kind machine has none of those hours yet.

Redundant, hot-swappable subsystems and N+1 design
Condition monitoring to convert unplanned outages into planned ones
Component lifetime characterisation under the 5.44% neutron load
Modular replacement to shorten outage duration

Even improved, an early burner is best paired with the grid or storage rather than sold as a sole Tier-III source. Claiming otherwise would contradict the model. The goal for 2032–2036 is credible, characterised availability — not a Tier-III guarantee on unproven hardware.

The honest core of this roadmap is that availability cannot be argued up; it must be measured up. Redundancy and modular replacement buy uptime immediately, but the 30–100x gap against Tier III only closes as fleet hours reveal and remove failure modes. Until that record exists, positioning Aegis as anything other than a paired source would contradict our own model.
See component lifetime and the availability gate in depth.

title: Why the Breeder Comes First
lede: The burner runs on helium-3 that only the breeder produces, so Hyperion's 2027 construction and 2030 first tritium set the earliest possible burner clock.
body: A fuel dependency, not a preference

Aegis cannot start before its fuel exists. Helium-3 at any useful scale comes from tritium decay, and the tritium comes from the breeder. Hyperion begins construction in Q2 2027 and targets FOAK first tritium around 2030. Only then does a burner fuel supply begin to accumulate.

Tritium decays to helium-3 with a fixed half-life; you cannot rush it. The breeder therefore produces a ~4 kg/yr tritium class and a ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 class on a schedule physics sets, not engineering. A test burner around 2032 uses this early, small supply; commercial fleets need a breeder fleet.
Every burner date is anchored to a breeder date. If breeder first tritium slips, the test burner and commercial burner slip with it. This is the honest reason the burner is not promised sooner.

This dependency is often the first surprise for a reader who meets the burner alone: it is not a standalone machine. Its resilience story — sovereign power free of the fuel-logistics tail — depends entirely on a domestic breeder loop that must exist first. The tandem-mirror core can be admired in isolation, but its fuel cannot, and we present the two together for that reason.
See the helium-3 supply gate and helium-3 from the breeder.

The breeder treats tritium breeding ratio (TBR) as a design lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8. A higher TBR means more tritium bred per fusion, which — after decay — means more helium-3 for burners. The chosen TBR shapes how quickly a burner fuel supply can grow.
Why the burner waits on it
Until FOAK proves breeding in hardware, the helium-3 supply for Aegis is a projection. FOAK converts that projection into a measured breeding rate, which is what a test burner around 2032 depends on.

FOAK is the moment a projection becomes a measured rate. Until the first-of-a-kind breeder breeds tritium in hardware, the burner's helium-3 supply is an estimate resting on the chosen tritium breeding ratio; after FOAK, it rests on a number the machine actually produced. That is why we tie the burner's earliest possible date to a breeder milestone rather than to a burner one.
See the TBR lever and no net gain before FOAK.

The test burner earns its place by converting the two hardest gates — plug feasibility and regime distance — from projections into measurements. It is sized to operate near the design point, not at commercial scale, precisely so that the physics can be learned before the engineering is committed. Everything it measures feeds the ~2036 commercial decision; nothing about that decision is assumed before it runs.

title: The Commercial Burner (~2036)
lede: A commercial-scale burner around 2036 is targeted only after the test burner supplies the operating data that closes the four gates.
body: A gated, not a scheduled, milestone

The commercial burner, targeted around 2036 at a roughly 1 GW fleet scale, is conditional. It follows the test burner only if that machine demonstrates a survivable plug, a measured regime, workable direct energy conversion, and characterised component life. The date is a target that the physics must earn.

title: From Simulation to Test Burner
lede: The bridge years between today's models and the ~2032 test burner: coupon magnets, regime experiments, and a fuel supply that has just begun.
body: What has to happen in between

There is real work between a design study and a test machine. Between now and ~2032 the plug coil must move from a 3–3.9x overstress result to a tested coupon; the regime must be walked outward in experiments; and the breeder must reach FOAK so that any burner fuel exists.

These threads run in parallel. Magnet, plasma-physics, fuel-supply, and materials programs advance together because a test burner needs all of them at once. The breeder's 2030 first tritium is the pacing item for fuel; the magnet program is the pacing item for the plug.
The bridge ends when an integrated machine can be built with a survivable coil, a fuel supply, and codes validated close enough to the design point to be trusted. That machine is the test burner.

The bridge years are where a design study either becomes an engineering program or reveals that it cannot. Running the magnet, plasma-physics, fuel-supply, and materials threads in parallel is not efficiency for its own sake; a test burner needs all of them at once, so a lag in any one is a lag in the machine. The breeder paces fuel; the magnet program paces the plug.

title: The Validation Campaign
lede: A structured plan to turn modelled claims into measured ones, subsystem by subsystem, from coupon tests through the test burner.
body: Validation is organised by subsystem and by increasing integration. Each subsystem is first tested alone, then in combination, then in the integrated test burner. A claim is only promoted from simulated to demonstrated when a physical test supports it.

Staging protects against compounding optimism. If the plug coil coupon does not meet margin, that is known before an integrated machine depends on it. The campaign is the discipline that keeps the 2032 and 2036 dates honest.

Staging the campaign is the mechanism that keeps optimism from compounding. If a magnet coupon misses margin, that is known before an integrated machine depends on it, and the design responds rather than the schedule pretending. A result outside its predicted band is treated as data that re-informs the models, not as an inconvenience to be smoothed over.

title: The Plug-Coil Prototype Program
lede: A staged magnet program to take the plug coil from a 3-to-3.9x overstress result to a demonstrated, field-bearing coil.
body: The plug coil is the machine's hardest structural requirement. The prototype program builds up in scale: material coupons, sub-scale windings, then a representative coil section tested to the modelled 26.49 T field and its associated stress.

Coupons: do the alloys and conductor meet the assumed strength and fatigue?
Sub-scale: can the winding carry the current density with margin?
Coil section: does a real geometry survive the modelled stress at field?
Prototype: does the plug hold 26.49 T at the design bore?
The go/no-go for the test burner

A test burner around 2032 cannot be committed until a plug prototype demonstrates margin. This program is therefore on the critical path, and its results directly determine whether the plug-stress gate is closing.

This program sits on the critical path because the plug is the machine's single hardest structural requirement. A test burner cannot be committed until a prototype coil demonstrates margin at or near 26.49 T, so the prototype schedule effectively sets the earliest credible test-burner date. Progress here is the clearest single indicator of whether the plug-stress gate is genuinely closing.
See magnet readiness and closing the plug-stress gate.

title: High-Field Magnet Readiness
lede: The 26.49 T plug and 17 T throat sit at the frontier of superconducting magnet technology; their readiness is the pacing item for burner hardware.
body: Aegis needs 26.49 T at the plug and 17 T at the throat. These are extreme fields; the plug in particular exceeds what any fielded fusion magnet holds today, and at the design bore the coil is overstressed 3–3.9x. Magnet readiness is therefore the single most limiting hardware question.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><text x="250" y="33" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Throat field</text><rect x="258" y="21" width="304.4" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="568.4" y="33" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">17 T</text><text x="250" y="67" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Plug field</text><rect x="258" y="55" width="352.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="616.0" y="67" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">26.49 T (overstressed)</text></svg>

High-temperature superconductor (REBCO) tape enables high fields, but field alone is not the problem — structure is. Running REBCO at conservative current density buys stress margin in exchange for more conductor. The trade between field, bore, current density, and structure is the heart of the magnet program.

No magnet at 26.49 T with the required bore and margin has been demonstrated. Until a coil section is tested, the plug field remains a simulation target. This is stated plainly because it is the gate most likely to move the schedule.

It is worth separating two ideas that are easily conflated: reaching a field and surviving it. High-temperature superconductor makes 26.49 T conceivable, but the binding problem is structural, not electromagnetic. The magnet program therefore spends most of its effort on the field/bore/current-density/structure trade, and treats a tested coil section — not a computed field — as the milestone that matters.

title: Regime-Scaling Experiments
lede: Experiments that walk the plug operating point outward, step by step, to reduce the 166-to-830x extrapolation to a validated range.
body: A single leap to the Aegis point would produce data no code predicted, teaching little about why. Stepwise campaigns instead advance the operating point in controlled increments, re-validating models at each step so the final extrapolation is short and understood.

Transport and confinement scaling with plug parameters
Onset of any micro-instabilities not seen at lower parameters
Discrepancies between code prediction and measurement, with bounds
Whether direct energy conversion efficiency holds as the regime shifts

The gate is not closed by reaching the design point in one experiment; it is closed by a chain of steps that leave a short, validated extrapolation. The test burner around 2032 is the last and largest step before commercial confidence.

The end state these experiments aim for is a validated band, not a single hero shot at the design point. A chain of steps, each re-validating the codes, leaves a short and defensible extrapolation; a single leap leaves an unexplained result. The test burner is the last and largest step in that chain, and it is where the remaining distance is meant to be small.

title: The Helium-3 Supply Ramp
lede: How the fuel supply grows from the first bred grams to fleet-scale demand: breeder output first, lunar helium-3 as fleets exceed it.
body: Matching supply to demand over time

Burner demand grows in steps — a small test-burner draw around 2032, then fleet-scale demand around 2036 and beyond. Supply must lead demand. The breeder produces the first helium-3 (~1.97 kg/yr class per unit, from ~4 kg/yr tritium), and the breeder fleet is sized to the burners it feeds.

The three sources in priority order
Breeder-bred helium-3: the only near-term source, domestic and controllable
A growing breeder fleet: scales fuel with the number of breeders built
Lunar helium-3: a multi-decade reservoir for demand beyond the breeder fleet
A single commercial unit needs ~400x today's domestic supply, so the ramp is steep. The honest position is that fleet-scale burner deployment is gated on this ramp, not the other way around.

The ramp is steep because the starting point is so low: today's domestic helium-3 is measured in small quantities, while one commercial unit needs about 400x that supply. Supply must therefore lead demand at every stage, which is why the breeder fleet is sized to the burners it feeds and why lunar recovery, however distant, is kept in the plan as the fleet-scale reservoir.
See the fuel gate and lunar dependency.

title: The Lunar Helium-3 Dependency
lede: Beyond a breeder fleet, lunar helium-3 is the only known reservoir at fleet scale; it is a multi-decade dependency, stated as such.
body: When the Moon enters the plan

Breeder-bred helium-3 covers the test burner and early commercial units. Once burner fleets scale beyond what a breeder fleet can feed, the only known reservoir large enough is lunar regolith. This is a long-horizon dependency — recovery, processing, and return logistics are all unproven — and we do not present it as near-term.

title: The Availability Improvement Roadmap
lede: From modelled 0.86-to-0.995 toward trustworthy uptime: the sequence of redundancy, operating hours, and honest positioning against Tier III.
body: Modelled availability of 0.86–0.995 is 30–100x short of Tier III (0.99982). No design change alone closes that; it takes operating hours from real machines. The roadmap therefore front-loads learning and redundancy, and is candid that early units are not sole Tier-III sources.

Design in redundancy and modular replacement from the first unit
Instrument everything so outages become predictable and planned
Characterise component life under the 5.44% neutron fraction
Accumulate fleet hours; remove the failure modes they reveal
The credible near-term goal is characterised, improving availability paired with grid or storage — not a Tier-III guarantee. Overpromising here would contradict our own model and erode trust.

The roadmap front-loads learning because availability is the one gate that cannot be closed by analysis at all. Redundancy and instrumentation raise the floor immediately, and component-life characterisation under the 5.44% neutron load sharpens the estimates, but only accumulated fleet hours remove the failure modes that separate 0.86–0.995 from Tier III. We say so plainly rather than implying a paper path to 0.99982.
See the availability gate and component lifetime.

title: Neutron Fraction and Material Readiness
lede: The 5.44% neutron fraction is low but not zero; qualifying materials for it is part of readiness, not an afterthought.
body: D–3He is often called clean, but Aegis carries a 5.44% neutron fraction from side reactions. That is far below a D–T machine, yet high enough to drive material damage, activation, and component wear that must be characterised before availability and lifetime can be trusted.

First-wall and plasma-facing materials under 14 MeV-relevant flux
Activation and handling of neutron-exposed components
Insulation and structural degradation over service life
Shielding sufficient to protect coils and personnel

Material qualification feeds directly into the availability and lifetime gates: you cannot state a maintenance interval you have not measured. The test burner around 2032 is where these materials first see real flux.

Describing D–³He as clean is only half true, and we keep the other half in view. A 5.44% neutron fraction is far below a D–T machine, but it still activates components, damages structure, and sets shielding requirements. Qualifying materials for that flux is not housekeeping; it is a precondition for any honest statement about component lifetime and therefore about availability.
See component lifetime and neutron fraction and fuel choice.

title: Direct Energy Conversion Readiness
lede: Converting charged particles straight to electricity has bench heritage but must be shown at Aegis scale and power before it counts as demonstrated.
body: Direct energy conversion (DEC) captures the kinetic energy of charged fusion products as electricity, skipping the steam cycle. Small-scale DEC has been demonstrated in earlier mirror work, which is why it sits at mid readiness — higher than the plug magnet, lower than the underlying physics.

Conversion efficiency at Aegis power, not bench power
Grid and collector survival under continuous high flux
Behaviour with the 5.44% neutron background present

The principle is not in doubt; the scale is. The test burner around 2032 is where DEC efficiency is measured under representative conditions. Until then, quoted efficiencies are modelled.

Direct energy conversion is the subsystem where heritage and scale diverge most sharply. The principle has been shown in small mirror experiments, which is why it sits above the plug magnet in readiness, but efficiency at Aegis power under a real neutron background is unmeasured. Quoted conversion efficiencies are therefore modelled, and the test burner is where they first meet representative conditions.
See DEC balance of plant and integrated systems test.

title: The Integrated Systems Test
lede: Before commercial commitment, the whole fuel-to-electricity chain must run together; the test burner is that integrated test.
body: Why integration is its own gate

Subsystems can each pass alone and still fail together. Integration reveals interactions — magnet cooling under plasma load, DEC behaviour with real neutron background, fuel handling at operating rate — that no single-subsystem test can show. The test burner around 2032 is the first integrated run.

Integrated results are the evidence base for the ~2036 commercial decision. A subsystem that passed alone but fails in integration is exactly the kind of finding this test exists to surface early.

Integration is its own gate because subsystems interact in ways single-subsystem tests cannot reveal: magnet cooling under plasma load, conversion behaviour with real neutron background, fuel handling at operating rate. A component that passes alone and fails in combination is exactly the finding an integrated test exists to surface — early, on a learning machine, rather than late, on a commercial one.

title: Commissioning and First-Burn Readiness
lede: The steps that take an assembled test burner from cold hardware to a first controlled burn, with safety and protection proven first.
body: Commissioning walks a machine up in stages: vacuum and leak checks, magnet cool-down and energisation, subsystem checkouts, then progressively longer plasma shots toward a first controlled burn. Each stage has hold points that must pass before the next begins.

Radiological monitoring for the 5.44% neutron output active
Control-room procedures rehearsed on the training simulator
Why first burn is not net gain

A first controlled burn demonstrates the machine can operate; it is not a net-gain claim. Performance is measured over a campaign, not declared at first light. The honest milestone remains the breeder FOAK for hardware net-gain relevance.

A first controlled burn is a demonstration of operability, not a performance claim, and we are careful to keep the two apart. Performance is measured across a campaign; first light only shows the machine can be brought up safely. Safety and protection systems are proven before high field precisely because the honest sequence puts interlocks ahead of records.
See readiness and first burn and no net gain before FOAK.

title: No Net-Gain Claim Before FOAK
lede: We make no hardware net-gain claim before the breeder first-of-a-kind first tritium around 2030; the burner claims nothing before its own test data.
body: The rule, stated once and kept

No machine on this program has produced net energy, and we do not claim it will before it is shown. The first hardware milestone relevant to net gain is the breeder FOAK first tritium around 2030. The burner makes no net-gain claim before its test burner around 2032 produces data, and no commercial performance claim before ~2036.

title: Design-Point Freeze and Change Control
lede: The Aegis numbers are a frozen design point under change control, so quoted figures stay consistent across the whole microsite.
body: A moving design point makes honesty impossible; readers cannot tell a real update from a quiet revision. Aegis therefore works from a frozen canonical design point — 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, 5.44% neutron fraction, ~90 keV — and every page quotes those exact figures.

Freezing protects the reader. If the plug field or neutron fraction changed silently, the four gates would no longer mean what the pages say. The freeze is a trust mechanism, not a bureaucratic one.

Freezing the numbers is a service to the reader, not a bureaucratic reflex. If the plug field or neutron fraction drifted silently, the four gates would no longer mean what the pages say they mean. Change control makes any revision a visible, logged event that recomputes the affected gates and updates dependent pages together, so no two pages ever disagree about a canonical figure.

title: The Open-Items Risk Register
lede: A single list of the burner's open technical risks, each tied to the gate it belongs to and the milestone that would retire it.
body: One place for the honest risks

Scattered caveats are easy to lose. The register collects the burner's open items in one place, each mapped to a gate and a milestone. Nothing here is economic; every item is a physics or engineering unknown.

A register is more honest than scattered caveats because it forces every open item into one comparable list, each tied to the gate it belongs to and the milestone that would retire it. Nothing here is economic; every entry is a physics or engineering unknown. An item leaves the register only when hardware supports it, mirroring the simulated-versus-demonstrated ledger elsewhere in this section.

title: Open Question: Is the Plug Feasible?
lede: The most consequential open question is whether a coil can hold 26.49 T at the design bore; today it is overstressed 3 to 3.9 times.
body: Can a real magnet produce and survive 26.49 T at the bore the design needs? Today the answer in simulation is no — the coil is overstressed 3–3.9x. This is the question most likely to reshape the machine or the schedule.

A materials and structure combination that reaches margin at 26.49 T
A field/bore re-optimisation that lowers peak stress
A confinement scheme that tolerates a lower plug field
An honest conclusion that the design point must move
Why we state it as open

We do not assume the plug is solvable at the current point. Stating it as an open question — with a real chance the design point changes — is more honest than presenting the 26.49 T plug as settled. The prototype program exists to answer it.

We state this as a genuine question, with a real possibility that the answer forces the design point to move, because that is the honest posture. A study that assumed the plug solvable at 26.49 T would be asserting the very thing it has not shown. The prototype program exists to answer the question in hardware, and we will report whichever way it answers.
See plug feasibility in depth and the prototype program.

title: Open Question: Will Helium-3 Yield Suffice?
lede: Whether bred and lunar helium-3 can close a 400x per-unit supply gap in time is a genuine open question, not a solved one.
body: A commercial unit needs about 400x today's domestic helium-3. The breeder produces a ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 class per unit from a ~4 kg/yr tritium class; the tritium breeding ratio lever (1.1/1.5/1.8) shapes the rate. The open question is whether a breeder fleet, then lunar recovery, can scale fast enough to feed burner fleets.

How large a breeder fleet must be per burner it feeds
How quickly breeders can be built and fuelled
Whether lunar recovery matures on any relevant horizon
Handling losses that erode usable yield
We present fleet-scale burner deployment as gated on this yield, not as assured. The breeder makes the fuel real; lunar helium-3 makes fleet scale conceivable; neither is a guarantee of rate.

The uncertainty here is compound: breeder build rate, fleet size per burner, handling losses, and the distant maturity of lunar recovery all multiply. Presenting fleet-scale burner deployment as gated on yield — rather than as assured — is the only claim the evidence supports. The breeder makes the fuel real; whether it can be made real fast enough is not yet settled.
See the supply ramp and the TBR lever.

title: Open Question: Can Availability Reach Data-Center Uptime?
lede: Whether a burner can ever meet hyperscale Tier III uptime is unanswered; today the model is 30 to 100x short.
body: Can a fusion machine reach 0.99982 availability? Modelled Aegis availability is 0.86–0.995, a 30–100x downtime gap. No fusion machine has the operating hours to answer this, so it is genuinely open — and we do not pretend otherwise by selling Aegis as a sole Tier-III source today.

Fleet operating hours that expose and remove failure modes
Component lifetimes measured under the 5.44% neutron load
Redundancy that turns single-point failures into ride-throughs
Predictable, planned maintenance replacing unplanned outages

The credible near-term claim is improving, characterised availability paired with grid or storage — not a Tier-III guarantee. Whether the gap fully closes is a question only operating fleets can answer.

No fusion machine has the operating hours to answer whether Tier III uptime is reachable, so we decline to answer it in advance. The credible near-term claim is improving, characterised availability paired with grid or storage. Whether the 30–100x gap ever fully closes is a question that only operating fleets can settle, and we present it as open rather than solved.

title: Verification and Validation Methodology
lede: How we separate a code that runs correctly (verification) from a code that matches reality (validation), and why both matter for the gates.
body: Verification asks: does the code solve its equations correctly? Validation asks: do those equations match the real machine? A verified but unvalidated code can be confidently wrong — which is exactly the risk in the 166–830x regime, where no validating data exists yet.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="6.0" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="81.2" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Verification</text><text x="81.2" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">code is correct</text><line x1="156.5" y1="69" x2="174.5" y2="69" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="178.5" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="253.8" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Validation</text><text x="253.8" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">matches data</text><line x1="329.0" y1="69" x2="347.0" y2="69" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="351.0" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="426.2" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Extrapolation</text><text x="426.2" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">bounded reach</text><line x1="501.5" y1="69" x2="519.5" y2="69" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="523.5" y="42" width="150.5" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="598.8" y="64" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12" font-weight="600">Prediction</text><text x="598.8" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">with uncertainty</text></svg>
Verify solvers against analytic and benchmark cases
Validate against every operated device we can
Bound extrapolation distance explicitly (the regime multiplier)
Attach uncertainty to every prediction, not just a point value

The gates are only as honest as the codes behind them. Stating that the plug regime is un-post-dictable is itself a V&V statement: no validating data exists at that point. The test burner is the first machine that adds validating data near the design regime.

The distinction between verification and validation is not academic here; it is the difference between a code that is confidently right and one that is confidently wrong. In the 166–830x regime no validating data exists, so even a perfectly verified code can only extrapolate. Saying the plug regime is un-post-dictable is itself a validation statement, and it is why the test burner matters.

title: Code Benchmarking Status
lede: Where the physics and engineering codes stand: benchmarked against known cases, validated only within the range of operated devices.
body: The equilibrium, transport, neutronics, and structural codes are checked against analytic solutions and against each other. That establishes they compute what they claim. It does not establish that the answers hold at the Aegis operating point.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><rect x="8" y="8.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M10,18.0 l4,4 l7,-9" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="20.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Solvers verified against analytic cases</text><rect x="8" y="34.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M10,44.0 l4,4 l7,-9" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="46.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Cross-code agreement on shared problems</text><rect x="8" y="60.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.4"/><circle cx="15" cy="69.0" r="3.5" fill="#9FB1C4"/><text x="34" y="72.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Validated within operated-device range</text><rect x="8" y="86.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="98.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Validated near the plug design regime</text><rect x="8" y="112.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="124.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Validated at the 26.49 T plug structurally</text></svg>

Validation ends where operated devices end. Beyond that — the 166–830x regime, the 26.49 T plug — the codes extrapolate. We label such results as extrapolations with uncertainty, never as validated predictions.
Each regime-scaling experiment and, later, the test burner extends the validated range. Code benchmarking status is therefore a moving line that the validation campaign pushes outward.

The honest boundary is the range of operated devices; beyond it, the codes extrapolate and we label them as doing so. That boundary is not fixed — each regime-scaling experiment and, later, the test burner push it outward — but at any moment it defines which of our numbers are validated and which are projections. Reporting the boundary is as important as reporting the numbers.

title: Uncertainty Quantification
lede: Every modelled figure carries uncertainty; we attach bounds rather than quote single numbers as if they were measured.
body: A modelled result quoted as a bare number invites the reader to treat it as measured. We instead attach uncertainty: the plug regime is 166–830x (a range, not a point), availability is 0.86–0.995, plug overstress is 3–3.9x. Ranges are the honest form for a design study.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><text x="250" y="33" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Plug regime range</text><rect x="258" y="21" width="342.8" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="606.8" y="33" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">166–830x</text><text x="250" y="67" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Availability range</text><rect x="258" y="55" width="352.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="616.0" y="67" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">0.86–0.995</text><text x="250" y="101" text-anchor="end" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">Plug overstress</text><rect x="258" y="89" width="69.4" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.85"/><text x="333.4" y="101" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5" font-weight="600">3–3.9x</text></svg>
Model form: which physics the code includes or omits
Inputs: material properties, cross-sections, geometry tolerances
Extrapolation distance: larger reach, larger uncertainty
Integration effects not captured in single-subsystem models

Uncertainty narrows with data. Coupon tests shrink the magnet range; regime experiments shrink the confinement range; fleet hours shrink availability. The test burner is the largest single reducer of uncertainty before commercial commitment.

Quoting ranges rather than single numbers is a deliberate refusal to let a modelled figure pose as a measured one. The plug regime is 166–830x, availability is 0.86–0.995, plug overstress is 3–3.9x; each range carries its worst case in plain sight. Ranges narrow only as data arrives, and the test burner is the single largest reducer of uncertainty before any commercial commitment.

title: Test-Burner Success Criteria
lede: The specific, measurable outcomes the ~2032 test burner must produce to justify a commercial decision around 2036.
body: The test burner succeeds if it converts the four gates from projections into data. Success is not a single burn; it is a campaign that measures the plug, the regime, the conversion, and component behaviour under real conditions.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><rect x="8" y="8.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="20.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Plug coil holds field with measured margin</text><rect x="8" y="34.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="46.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Confinement measured near design regime</text><rect x="8" y="60.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="72.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">DEC efficiency measured at scale</text><rect x="8" y="86.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="98.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Component wear under 5.44% neutrons characterised</text><rect x="8" y="112.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="124.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Repeatable, controlled operation demonstrated</text></svg>
Regime extrapolation reduced from 166–830x to a validated band
Plug stress margin demonstrated at or near 26.49 T
DEC efficiency within the modelled uncertainty range
Maintenance intervals estimated from real wear data
If a criterion is missed, that is a finding that reshapes the commercial design or its schedule — not a result to bury. The criteria exist so success and failure are both legible in advance.

Writing the criteria in advance means success and failure are both legible before the machine runs, which is the point. A missed criterion is not an outcome to bury; it reshapes the commercial design or its schedule. Each threshold ties directly to a gate — regime band, plug margin, conversion efficiency, measured wear — so the campaign's results map cleanly onto the ~2036 decision.

title: Commercial Readiness Criteria
lede: What must be true across all four gates before a commercial burner around 2036 can be committed.
body: Commercial readiness is stricter than test-burner success. It requires not just that the physics works once, but that it works repeatably, at fleet-relevant fuel supply, with characterised availability and lifetime. All four gates must show durable resolution.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><rect x="8" y="8.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="20.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Plug feasibility demonstrated and repeatable</text><rect x="8" y="34.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="46.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Regime validated at the design point</text><rect x="8" y="60.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="72.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Fuel supply path to fleet demand established</text><rect x="8" y="86.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="98.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Availability characterised and honestly positioned</text><rect x="8" y="112.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="124.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Component lifetimes support a maintenance plan</text></svg>

Commercial also means the same D–<sup>3</sup>He core can be fielded in both housings — Aegis for fixed defense installations and MetroVolt for data centers — with a manufacturing and supply chain able to build more than one. A single working machine is necessary but not sufficient.
If any gate remains open, the commercial date moves. 2036 is a target contingent on the evidence, and we say so rather than presenting it as fixed.

The commercial bar is stricter than test-burner success because it demands repeatability, fleet-relevant fuel supply, and characterised lifetimes, not a single working run. It also demands a supply chain able to build more than one machine across both the Aegis and MetroVolt housings. If any gate remains open at the decision point, the honest response is to move the date, and we say so.

title: Staged Deployment: FOAK, NOAK, BOAK
lede: Even after the first commercial burner, deployment is staged first-of-a-kind, then nth-of-a-kind, then best-of-a-kind, so each unit learns from the last.
body: The first commercial machine is still a first. Staged deployment — first-of-a-kind (FOAK), then nth-of-a-kind (NOAK), then best-of-a-kind (BOAK) — means each unit incorporates operating lessons from those before it, especially on availability and component life.

Availability, as failure modes are removed with fleet hours
Maintenance intervals, as component wear is measured
Fuel efficiency in handling, tightening the ³He balance
Build repeatability across both Aegis and MetroVolt housings
This mirrors the breeder's own FOAK→NOAK→BOAK progression. The two fleets scale together: breeder units feed burner units, and both mature through the same staged learning.

Staging continues after the first commercial machine because that machine is still a first, with unproven availability and unmeasured lifetimes. Each subsequent unit incorporates operating lessons from those before it, so the fleet improves as it grows. title: What Would Falsify the Design
lede: Named experiments and outcomes that would prove the current burner design point wrong, stated in advance so the study is testable.
body: A testable design, not an unfalsifiable one

A design study earns trust by naming what would refute it. For Aegis, several concrete outcomes would falsify the current design point and force a redesign or a different machine — and we would report them as such.

<svg viewBox="0 0 680 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><rect x="8" y="8.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="20.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">No coil reaches 26.49 T margin → plug point falsified</text><rect x="8" y="34.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="46.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Regime experiments reveal fatal loss channels</text><rect x="8" y="60.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="72.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">DEC efficiency collapses at scale</text><rect x="8" y="86.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="98.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Component life too short for any maintenance plan</text><rect x="8" y="112.0" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#3A4656" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="34" y="124.0" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11.5">Fuel supply cannot reach unit demand on any horizon</text></svg>

Unfalsifiable claims are not science. By listing the outcomes that would end the current design, we commit to following the evidence — including evidence that the 26.49 T plug or the design regime cannot be reached as specified.

A falsified point does not necessarily end the program; it moves the design. The tandem-mirror core, the D–<sup>3</sup>He fuel, and direct energy conversion could survive a plug redesign. Honesty about falsification is how the study improves.

Naming what would refute the design is what separates a testable study from an unfalsifiable claim. If no coil reaches margin at 26.49 T, or if regime experiments reveal fatal loss channels, the current design point is falsified and we will report it as such. A falsification moves the design; it need not end the program, since the tandem-mirror core and D–³He fuel could survive a plug redesign.

title: The Readiness Scorecard
lede: A single graded view of every subsystem and gate, on the same ruler, so nothing is hidden and nothing is overstated.
body: The scorecard grades every element of the burner on the same scale: established, simulated, or open. It puts the mature physics and the open gates side by side so a reader sees the whole picture, not a curated slice.

Simulated — supported only by models today
Open — not yet supported by either; a gate to close

A graded table resists cherry-picking. The mature rows do not excuse the open ones, and the open rows do not erase the mature ones. This is the honest summary the rest of the section supports in detail.

The scorecard's discipline is that everything is graded on one ruler, so mature rows cannot excuse open ones and open rows cannot erase mature ones. A reader gets the whole picture in a single view rather than a curated slice. The detailed pages in this section exist to justify each grade, and the grades change only when hardware evidence justifies the change.

title: How to Read Our Honest Gates
lede: A short guide to interpreting the gate figures: what they are, what they are not, and why we never translate them into cost.
body: Each gate figure is a physics or engineering result from our models: 3–3.9x plug overstress, 166–830x regime distance, ~400x fuel gap, 30–100x availability shortfall against 0.99982. They quantify the distance between the current design and a fielded machine.

lede: Availability and maintenance plans depend on component lifetimes that no burner has yet accumulated; measuring them is a readiness task.

title: Reliability and Redundancy Readiness
lede: Redundant, hot-swappable design is how an early burner narrows the availability gap while its component lifetimes are still being learned.
body: Design for the uptime you cannot yet prove

With component lifetimes unmeasured, redundancy is the near-term lever on availability. N+1 subsystems, hot-swappable modules, and fast fault isolation let the plant ride through failures that would otherwise become outages — buying uptime before fleet hours exist.

title: A Short Readiness Glossary
lede: Plain definitions of the readiness terms used across this section, so the honest claims are unambiguous.
body: Design-and-simulation stage — the machine exists only in models; every number is computed, not measured
FOAK / NOAK / BOAK — first-, nth-, and best-of-a-kind units in a staged build
TRL — technology readiness level, 1 (principles) to 9 (proven in operation)
Gate — a quantified physics or engineering distance between the current design and a fielded machine
Post-diction — reproducing a device already operated; the basis for trusting an extrapolation
Plug overstress (3–3.9x) — coil stress above allowable at the 26.49 T design bore
Regime distance (166–830x) — how far the plug point sits beyond any operated device
Fuel gap (~400x) — unit helium-3 demand versus today's domestic supply
Availability shortfall (30–100x) — modelled downtime versus Tier III (0.99982)
Construction (breeder, Q2 2027), first tritium (breeder FOAK, ~2030), test burner (~2032), commercial burner (~2036). Each later date is contingent on the earlier milestone's evidence.

These definitions are collected so that the honest claims elsewhere in the section cannot be misread. Where a term carries a number — 3–3.9x, 166–830x, ~400x, 30–100x against 0.99982 — the number is the frozen canonical value, quoted identically wherever it appears. When a page says a result is simulated rather than demonstrated, these definitions are what that distinction rests on.
See how to read the gates and the overview.
